claims.claim: Töyrylä says Kay uses a matter-of-fact style to describe a dramatic and violent event in Tigana.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, BA thesis, University of Helsinki (2017)
claims.quote: Again a matter-of-fact style is used to describe a dramatic and violent event

claims.claim: Töyrylä describes that passage's narrator as merely reporting what happened without any commentary.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, BA thesis, University of Helsinki (2017)
claims.quote: the narrator is merely reporting what happened, without any commentary

claims.claim: Töyrylä reads the phrase 'according to most reports later' as the narrator restricting his omniscience to what people hear about the incident afterwards.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, BA thesis, University of Helsinki (2017)
claims.quote: narrating only what people hear about the incident afterwards

claims.claim: Töyrylä argues that a shift out of a character's perspective is what lets Kay describe that character's execution matter-of-factly.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, BA thesis, University of Helsinki (2017)
claims.quote: enables the matter-of-fact description of his execution

claims.claim: Töyrylä argues that Kay's narrator describes things as an inhabitant of the storyworld would rather than as an outsider.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, BA thesis, University of Helsinki (2017)
claims.quote: the narrator describes things like an inhabitant of that world would

claims.claim: Töyrylä finds that in passages using the phrase 'as everyone knows' the narrator's perspective coincides with that of an average citizen of the Palm.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, BA thesis, University of Helsinki (2017)
claims.quote: concurs with that of an average citizen of the Palm

claims.claim: Hatch argues that through the historian Pertennius Kay shows the historian's power outlasting that of the world's rulers.
claims.source: Jillian Hatch, University of Calgary undergraduate paper
claims.quote: the power of the historian is more lasting than that of the rulers of the world

claims.claim: Hatch reports that the narrator of Sailing to Sarantium claims on its first page that writers of history often seek the dramatic over the truth.
claims.source: Jillian Hatch, University of Calgary undergraduate paper, quoting Kay's Sailing to Sarantium p. 1
claims.quote: writers of history often seek the dramatic over the truth

claims.claim: Kleander counts twenty-one separate focalizants and more than 150 separate focalizations in Tigana, apart from the non-focalized narrative.
claims.source: Anya Kleander, Honours dissertation, University of Stirling (2008)
claims.quote: there are twenty-one separate focalizants in Tigana, and more than 150 separate focalizations

claims.claim: Kleander reports Kay as believing that the quiet, steady accumulation of detail and complexity reaches readers almost subliminally.
claims.source: Anya Kleander (2008) quoting Guy Gavriel Kay in an SF Site interview, 2000
claims.quote: quiet, steady accumulation of detail and complexity

claims.claim: Kay says he looks for the unwritten histories and the people at the margins of history.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay interviewed in Locus, 12 May 2025
claims.quote: the people at the margins of history

claims.claim: Kay says he also loves the chronicles of the dukes and the popes, alongside the unwritten lives of women and of the poor.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay interviewed in Locus, 12 May 2025
claims.quote: lives of women, and of the poor

claims.claim: Borowska-Szerszun argues that the restoration of Tigana's name remains marked by loss, fragmentation and incomplete knowledge.
claims.quote: it remains marked by loss, fragmentation, and incomplete knowledge

claims.claim: Johnston argues that Kay's reimagined ancient and medieval settings estrange the familiar, rendering it unheimlich.
claims.source: Susan A. Johnston, in Canadian Science Fiction, Fantasy, and Horror (Palgrave Macmillan, 2019)
claims.quote: estranging the familiar, rendering it unheimlich

claims.claim: Malosse argues that the Sarantine Mosaic, though deliberately unfaithful to history, evokes the Late Antique and Eastern Mediaeval world much more exactly than time-travel novels that respect history's givens.
claims.source: Pierre-Louis Malosse, Université Paul Valéry, Anabases 5 (2007)
claims.quote: evokes the Late Antique and Eastern Mediaeval world much more exactly

verdicts.trueWording: Again a matter-of-fact style is used to describe a dramatic and violent event
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the Toyryla thesis (brightweavings, bylined 'a bachelor's thesis by Roosa Toyryla, written at the University of Helsinki, Finland. 2017'), analysing the Senzio castle massacre in Tigana (Kay 722-23). The page phrases it passively ('a matter-of-fact style is used') and credits the narrator rather than naming Kay, but the text under analysis is Kay's Tigana.

verdicts.trueWording: the narrator is merely reporting what happened, without any commentary
verdicts.note: Verbatim; the full sentence continues 'and in the summary fashion of ambient focalization'. Same paragraph as index 195, so 'that passage's narrator' is correct.

verdicts.trueWording: narrating only what people hear about the incident afterwards
verdicts.note: Page: 'This is signalled by the phrase "according to most reports later"... The phrase also suggests that the narrator is restricting their omniscience and narrating only what people hear about the incident afterwards, not what is actually happening.' Only divergence: the thesis writes 'their omniscience', the claim writes 'his'.

verdicts.trueWording: This window shift distances the narration from Ettocio and enables the matter-of-fact description of his execution
verdicts.note: Verbatim, in the variable-internal-focalization section; the preceding sentence supplies the shift limb: 'The latter part of the above excerpt shifts from Ettocio's perspective to narratorial focalization.'

verdicts.trueWording: the narrator describes things like an inhabitant of that world would
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the communal-viewpoint section; the 'rather than as an outsider' limb is carried by the immediately preceding clause 'does not give the impression of being outside the story but inside it'.

verdicts.trueWording: Thus the narrator's perspective concurs with that of an average citizen of the Palm
verdicts.note: Verbatim, in the section headed 'Communal Viewpoints: As Everyone Knows'; the conclusion is drawn from the 'as everyone knows' phrase (Kay 65) - 'This comes most strongly across in the phrase "as everyone knows"'. The thesis argues it from that one excerpt inside a section about such passages generally.

verdicts.trueWording: Through his characterization of Pertennius, Kay illustrates the fact that the power of the historian is more lasting than that of the rulers of the world
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the Pertennius section of 'The Creative Construction of History in Guy Gavriel Kay's The Sarantine Mosaic', bylined 'by Jillian Hatch, 2005'. The page does not itself state the University of Calgary affiliation, but the claim sentence does not assert it.

verdicts.trueWording: Kay's narrator claims that, "writers of history often seek the dramatic over the truth" (Sailing 1)
verdicts.note: Verbatim in Hatch's final paragraph: 'At the end of the very first paragraph on the very first page of the first book in the Sarantine Mosaic...'; the page identifies Sailing to Sarantium as that first book.

verdicts.trueWording: In addition to the non-focalized narrative, there are twenty-one separate focalizants in Tigana, and more than 150 separate focalizations
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the numbered note (1) that closes the Tigana chapter of Anya Kleander's Stirling honours dissertation (page bylined 'a dissertation by Anya Kleander... at Stirling University, submitted in Spring 2008'). The note continues with Devin 41 and Dianora 27 focalizations.

verdicts.trueWording: Kay believes 'that the quiet, steady accumulation of detail and complexity reach out to readers in an almost subliminal way'
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the Sarantine Mosaic chapter, cited '(Kay in SFSite Interview 2000, url)'; the sentence continues 'and induces trust in the author and the book'.

verdicts.trueWording: I've talked often about looking for the unwritten histories, the people at the margins of history
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the interview excerpt published on the Locus site (12 May 2025, 'Guy Gavriel Kay: Margins of History'); the page carries only an excerpt, the full interview being in the May 2025 issue, but this passage is present on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: The unwritten lives of women, and of the poor. Though I do also love the chronicles of the dukes and the popes
verdicts.note: Verbatim, immediately after the index-205 sentence; Kay adds 'They are not exclusive ways of looking', which supports the claim's 'alongside'.

verdicts.trueWording: While the restoration of Tigana's name appears to reproduce a recognizably Tolkienian resolution, it remains marked by loss, fragmentation, and incomplete knowledge
verdicts.note: Wiley's live page is Cloudflare-blocked (HTTP 403); verified on the publisher-deposited abstract returned raw by Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1111/oli.70057) and matched word for word by OpenAlex. Article: 'The limits of the happy ending: Eucatastrophe and cultural memory in Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana', Sylwia Borowska-Szerszun, Orbis Litterarum, 2026-06-04.

verdicts.trueWording: novels that reimagine world history in alternate versions of ancient and medieval Europe and Asia, estranging the familiar, rendering it unheimlich: both home and not home at once
verdicts.note: link.springer.com serves only a JavaScript 'Client Challenge' to curl; verified on the raw Wayback capture https://web.archive.org/web/20191114214457id_/https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007%2F978-3-030-15685-5_7, whose chapter abstract carries the quote. Chapter 'When Are We Ever at Home? Exile and Nostalgia in the Work of Guy Gavriel Kay', Susan Johnston (Crossref gives no middle initial), Canadian Science Fiction, Fantasy, and Horror, 2019, pp. 119-133.

verdicts.trueWording: the Sarantine Mosaic, which is unfaithful to history and deliberately inverts and reconstructs historical matter, evokes the Late Antique and Eastern Mediaeval world much more exactly than the novels of de Camp and Silverberg, which endeavour to respect history's givens
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the concluding section of Morgon Mills's English translation of Pierre-Louis Malosse, 'Justinian Visited and Revisited' (Anabases 5, 2007, pp. 229-235), hosted at brightweavings. The comparanda are de Camp's Lest Darkness Fall and Silverberg's time-travel novel, both introduced earlier as time-travel narratives, so 'time-travel novels' holds. Note the source attaches 'deliberately' to 'inverts and reconstructs', not to 'unfaithful'.
